questions.question_text: Opportunity cost is best defined as:
questions.option_a: the money spent on a purchase
questions.option_b: the value of the next-best alternative forgone
questions.explanation: Opportunity cost is what you give up — the next-best alternative — not just the dollar price. Choosing to study means the forgone value of the best thing you could have done instead.

questions.question_text: A sunk cost is one that:
questions.option_a: should always be counted in decisions
questions.option_b: has already been incurred and cannot be recovered, so it should be ignored going forward
questions.explanation: Rational decisions look only at marginal benefits and costs going forward; sunk costs are irreversible and irrelevant to future choices. 'Throwing good money after bad' is the fallacy of honoring sunk costs.

questions.question_text: An increase in the price of a substitute good for coffee (e.g., tea) will:
questions.option_b: increase demand for coffee
questions.explanation: If tea gets pricier, consumers switch to coffee → coffee demand rises (shifts right). Substitutes' prices move a good's demand in the SAME direction; complements move it opposite.

questions.question_text: A surplus exists in a market when:
questions.option_b: price is above equilibrium, so quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded
questions.explanation: Above equilibrium, producers offer more than buyers want — a surplus that pushes price down toward equilibrium. Below equilibrium creates a shortage (the opposite).

questions.question_text: Demand for insulin is highly inelastic, meaning:
questions.option_a: quantity demanded responds strongly to price
questions.option_b: quantity demanded changes little when price changes
questions.explanation: Inelastic = quantity barely responds to price, typical of necessities with no substitutes (life-saving medicine). This is why sellers of necessities can raise prices without losing much volume.

questions.question_text: If demand is unit elastic, a price increase causes total revenue to:
questions.option_b: stay constant
questions.explanation: Unit elasticity (Ed = 1) means the percent change in quantity exactly offsets the percent change in price, so total revenue is unchanged. Revenue is maximized at this point on a linear demand curve.

questions.question_text: A normal good is one for which:
questions.option_b: demand rises as income rises
questions.explanation: Normal goods have positive income elasticity — higher income increases demand. Inferior goods (income elasticity negative) see demand FALL as income rises (e.g., bus rides as people buy cars).

questions.question_text: The law of diminishing marginal returns states that:
questions.option_b: adding more of a variable input to fixed inputs eventually yields smaller output increases
questions.option_d: all inputs are variable in the short run
questions.explanation: With at least one fixed input, each added worker eventually adds less extra output — diminishing marginal product. This rising marginal cost shapes the upward-sloping MC and supply curves.

questions.question_text: In the long run, all firms in perfect competition earn:
questions.option_b: zero economic profit due to free entry and exit
questions.explanation: Profits attract entry (driving price down) and losses cause exit (driving price up) until economic profit is zero. Firms still earn a normal profit (covering opportunity cost) — 'zero' is economic, not accounting.

questions.question_text: A perfectly competitive firm's demand curve is:
questions.option_b: perfectly elastic (horizontal) at the market price
questions.explanation: A price taker faces a horizontal demand curve — it can sell any quantity at the market price but nothing above it. This is why P = MR for competitive firms, unlike a monopoly's downward-sloping demand.

questions.question_text: Economies of scale occur when long-run average total cost:
questions.option_b: falls as output increases
questions.explanation: Economies of scale mean per-unit costs fall as the firm grows (spreading fixed costs, specialization). Diseconomies of scale (rising LRATC) eventually set in from coordination problems.

questions.question_text: A natural monopoly arises when:
questions.option_b: one firm can supply the entire market at lower cost than multiple firms (high fixed costs, economies of scale)
questions.explanation: Natural monopolies (utilities, water) have huge fixed costs and falling average costs over the relevant range, so a single firm is most efficient. This is why they're often regulated rather than broken up.

questions.question_text: Product differentiation is a key feature of:
questions.option_b: monopolistic competition
questions.explanation: Monopolistic competition has many firms selling differentiated (not identical) products, giving each a slight downward-sloping demand. Perfect competition assumes identical products; pure monopoly has one seller.

questions.question_text: For a monopolist, marginal revenue is less than price because:
questions.option_b: to sell one more unit it must lower price on all units
questions.explanation: A single-price monopolist lowers price on every unit to sell more, so the revenue from the extra unit (MR) is below its price. This MR < P gap is why monopolies underproduce relative to competition.

questions.question_text: Collusion among oligopoly firms is unstable mainly because:
questions.option_b: each firm has an incentive to cheat by secretly cutting price to gain market share
questions.explanation: A cartel sets high prices, but each member can profit by undercutting — the dominant-strategy incentive that breaks cartels (the prisoner's dilemma). This is why explicit collusion tends to collapse.

questions.question_text: A firm in a competitive labor market hires workers up to the point where:
questions.option_a: the wage equals marginal revenue product
questions.option_b: the wage equals total revenue
questions.explanation: Profit-maximizing hiring sets wage (the marginal cost of labor) equal to MRP (the marginal benefit). Beyond that point, each worker costs more than they add in revenue.

questions.question_text: The demand for labor is called a 'derived demand' because it depends on:
questions.option_b: the demand for the product the labor produces
questions.explanation: Firms hire workers to make products consumers want, so labor demand is DERIVED from product demand. If demand for cars falls, so does demand for autoworkers — regardless of wages.

questions.question_text: A firm using two inputs minimizes cost where:
questions.option_b: the ratio of marginal product to price is equal across inputs (MPL/PL = MPK/PK)
questions.explanation: Least-cost combination equalizes the 'bang per buck' — marginal product per dollar — across all inputs. Comparing raw marginal products ignores that inputs have different prices.

questions.question_text: A positive externality, like vaccination, leads the free market to:
questions.option_b: underproduce the good relative to the social optimum
questions.explanation: When benefits spill over to others (herd immunity), private buyers ignore the external benefit, so the market underproduces. A subsidy equal to the external benefit moves output toward the social optimum.

questions.question_text: A progressive tax is one where:
questions.option_a: everyone pays the same dollar amount
questions.option_b: the tax rate rises as income rises
questions.option_c: the tax rate falls as income rises
questions.explanation: Progressive taxes take a larger PERCENTAGE from higher incomes (e.g., the U.S. income tax). Regressive taxes (like sales tax as a share of income) fall harder on lower incomes; proportional is a flat rate.

questions.question_text: The Lorenz curve and Gini coefficient measure:
questions.option_b: income inequality within a population
questions.explanation: The Lorenz curve plots cumulative income share; the more it bows from the 45-degree line of perfect equality, the higher the Gini coefficient and the greater the inequality.

questions.question_text: The Coase theorem suggests that externalities can be resolved privately when:
questions.option_b: property rights are clearly defined and transaction costs are low
questions.explanation: Coase argued that with clear property rights and low bargaining costs, parties can negotiate an efficient outcome without government — e.g., a factory and residents trading pollution rights. High transaction costs break this.

questions.question_text: A movement ALONG a demand curve (vs a shift) is caused by a change in:
questions.option_b: the price of the good itself
questions.explanation: Only the good's OWN price changes quantity demanded (a movement along the curve). Income, substitute prices, and tastes shift the entire curve — a different concept the exam constantly tests.

questions.question_text: Consumer surplus is:
questions.option_a: the difference between what consumers pay and the cost of production
questions.option_b: the difference between what consumers are willing to pay and what they actually pay
questions.explanation: Consumer surplus is the area below the demand curve and above the price — the bonus buyers get from paying less than their maximum willingness to pay. Producer surplus is the mirror for sellers.

questions.question_text: A firm should shut down in the short run if price falls below:
questions.option_b: average variable cost
questions.explanation: If price can't even cover average variable cost, the firm loses more by operating than by shutting down (it still owes fixed costs either way). Between AVC and ATC, it operates at a loss but minimizes it.

questions.question_text: Price discrimination requires that a firm:
questions.option_a: sells in a perfectly competitive market
questions.option_b: has market power and can prevent resale between buyer groups
questions.explanation: To charge different prices (student vs adult tickets), a firm needs market power AND the ability to segment markets and block resale. Competitive price-takers can't price discriminate.

questions.question_text: Economic rent in a factor market refers to:
questions.option_b: payment to a factor above what is needed to keep it in its current use
questions.explanation: Economic rent is the surplus a resource earns beyond its opportunity cost — e.g., a star athlete's pay far above their next-best option. It's tied to inelastic factor supply.

questions.question_text: A common resource like ocean fish is prone to overuse because it is:
questions.option_b: non-excludable but rival (the tragedy of the commons)
questions.explanation: Common resources are rival (one person's catch reduces another's) but non-excludable (no one can be kept out), so each user overexploits — the tragedy of the commons. Public goods, by contrast, are non-rival.
